```{r}
reticulate::use_virtualenv("r-keras", required = TRUE)
library(tidyverse)

data <- readRDS("handwriting.rds")
images <- data$images
metadata <- as_tibble(data$metadata) %>%

stopifnot(

```

# Data exploration

The dataset contains 25,000 simulated grayscale images from 20 writers. Each image is 28 × 28 pixels, and each writer produced digits 0–4 across five sessions. We use it to compare closed-set writer identification with same-writer verification. These tasks use different test designs, so their accuracy values are not directly comparable.

## Structure and balance

The file contains an image array and one metadata row per image. Pixel values are integers from 0 to 255 and are divided by 255 before modelling. The checks below report the dimensions, pixel range, missing metadata, and balance across writers, digits, sessions, and writer–digit–session cells.

```{r}
cell_counts <- metadata %>% count(person_id, digit, session)
writer_counts <- metadata %>% count(person_id)
digit_counts <- metadata %>% count(digit)
session_counts <- metadata %>% count(session)

data_checks <- tibble(
  check = c(
    "Image array dimensions",
    "Scaled pixel range",
    "Pixels equal to background (0)",
    "Distinct pixel levels",
    "Missing metadata values",
    "Images per writer (min to max)",
    "Images per digit (min to max)",
    "Images per session (min to max)",
    "Images per writer-digit-session cell (min to max)"
  ),
  result = c(
    paste(dim(x), collapse = " x "),
    paste0(sprintf("%.0f", min(x)), " to ", sprintf("%.0f", max(x))),
    scales::percent(mean(x == 0), accuracy = 0.1),
    as.character(length(unique(as.vector(x)))),
    as.character(sum(is.na(metadata))),
    paste(range(writer_counts$n), collapse = " to "),
    paste(range(digit_counts$n), collapse = " to "),
    paste(range(session_counts$n), collapse = " to "),
    paste(range(cell_counts$n), collapse = " to ")
  )
)
knitr::kable(
  data_checks,
  col.names = c("Data check", "Result"),
  caption = "Image and metadata checks."
)
```

## What the images look like

The first grid shows one image per digit for five sampled writers in session 1. The second holds the writer and digit fixed and shows examples from each session.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "One sampled image per digit for five writers in session 1."
set.seed(5073)
shown_writers <- sample(sort(unique(metadata$person_id)), 5)
writer_digit_examples <- metadata %>%
  filter(person_id %in% shown_writers, session == 1) %>%
  group_by(person_id, digit) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 1) %>%
  ungroup()

pixels_for <- function(image_index) {
  img <- x[image_index, , , 1]
  expand_grid(row = 1:28, col = 1:28) %>%
    mutate(intensity = as.vector(t(img)))
}

plot_examples <- function(example_rows, facet_formula) {
  plot_data <- map2_dfr(
    example_rows$.image_index,
    seq_len(nrow(example_rows)),
    ~ pixels_for(.x) %>% mutate(panel = .y)
  ) %>%
    left_join(
      example_rows %>% mutate(panel = row_number()),
      by = "panel"
    )

  ggplot(plot_data, aes(col, row, fill = intensity)) +
    geom_raster() +
    scale_y_reverse() +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "black", guide = "none") +
    facet_grid(facet_formula, labeller = label_both) +
    coord_equal() +
    theme_void()
}

plot_examples(writer_digit_examples, person_id ~ digit)
```

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Examples of the same writer and digit across sessions."
set.seed(5073)
chosen_writer <- sample(sort(unique(metadata$person_id)), 1)
chosen_digit <- sample(sort(unique(metadata$digit)), 1)
session_examples <- metadata %>%
  filter(person_id == chosen_writer, digit == chosen_digit) %>%
  group_by(session) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 1) %>%
  ungroup()

plot_examples(session_examples, session ~ .)
```

In these examples, the strokes are centred on a mostly empty background. Slant and proportions vary between writers, while a writer’s digit can also change between sessions. Replicates within a writer–digit–session cell can look very similar. These are observations about the displayed examples, not measurements of every image.

## Limitations of the simulated data

The images do not represent the variation in pen, paper, cropping, and scanning found in real handwriting. There are only 20 writers and five digits, and each writer–digit–session cell has the same number of images. Replicates within a cell are related observations, so 25,000 images should not be treated as 25,000 independent writing styles. Conclusions below apply to this simulated dataset and the particular splits used.

# CNN writer identification

## Task, split, and model

The task is to predict one of 20 known writer IDs from a single 28 × 28 image. Writer IDs are coded 0–19 for the model. With balanced classes, chance accuracy is 1/20 (5%).

We trained on sessions 1–3 (15,000 images), used session 4 (5,000) for model selection, and reserved session 5 (5,000) for testing. Every writer and digit appears in each split. This tests whether the model recognises known writers in a later session, not whether it can identify a new writer.

The CNN has two convolution and max-pooling blocks (32 and 64 filters), followed by flattening, a 64-unit ReLU layer, dropout, and a 20-class softmax. It uses sparse categorical cross-entropy and Adam. We compared four combinations of dropout (0.2 or 0.4) and learning rate (0.001 or 0.0005), with batches of 64 and early stopping on session-4 validation accuracy (up to 15 epochs, patience 3). Session 5 was not used to select the model.

```{r}
train_idx <- which(metadata$session %in% 1:3)
valid_idx <- which(metadata$session == 4)
test_idx  <- which(metadata$session == 5)

y_writer <- as.integer(metadata$person_id) - 1L

build_cnn <- function(dropout_rate, learning_rate) {
  keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(28L, 28L, 1L)) %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 32L, kernel_size = 3L, padding = "same",
                  activation = "relu") %>%
    layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = 2L) %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 64L, kernel_size = 3L, padding = "same",
                  activation = "relu") %>%
    layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = 2L) %>%
    layer_flatten() %>%
    layer_dense(units = 64L, activation = "relu") %>%
    layer_dropout(rate = dropout_rate) %>%
    layer_dense(units = 20L, activation = "softmax") %>%
    compile(
      optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = learning_rate),
      loss = "sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
      metrics = "accuracy"
    )
}

cnn_grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  dropout = c(0.2, 0.4),
  learning_rate = c(0.001, 0.0005)
)
cnn_candidates <- map(seq_len(nrow(cnn_grid)), function(i) {
  set_random_seed(5073)
  model <- build_cnn(
    cnn_grid$dropout[i],
    cnn_grid$learning_rate[i]
  )
  history <- model %>% fit(
    x[train_idx, , , , drop = FALSE],
    y_writer[train_idx],
    validation_data = list(
      x[valid_idx, , , , drop = FALSE],
      y_writer[valid_idx]
    ),
    epochs = 15,
    batch_size = 64,
    callbacks = list(callback_early_stopping(
      monitor = "val_accuracy", mode = "max",
      patience = 3, restore_best_weights = TRUE
    )),
    verbose = 0
  )
  best_epoch <- which.max(history$metrics$val_accuracy)
  list(
    model = model,
    history = history,
    best_epoch = best_epoch
  )
})

cnn_tuning <- cnn_grid %>%
  mutate(
    best_validation_accuracy = map_dbl(
      cnn_candidates,
      ~ max(.x$history$metrics$val_accuracy, na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    validation_loss_at_best_accuracy = map_dbl(
      cnn_candidates,
      ~ .x$history$metrics$val_loss[[.x$best_epoch]]
    ),
    best_epoch = map_int(cnn_candidates, "best_epoch")
  )
best_cnn_index <- which.max(cnn_tuning$best_validation_accuracy)
cnn_tuning <- cnn_tuning %>%
  mutate(selected = row_number() == best_cnn_index)

ggplot(
  cnn_tuning,
  aes(
    x = factor(learning_rate),
    y = best_validation_accuracy,
    color = factor(dropout),
    group = factor(dropout)
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", best_validation_accuracy)),
    vjust = -0.8,
    show.legend = FALSE,
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("0.2" = "#3973ac", "0.4" = "#c65d3b"),
    name = "Dropout"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Best session-4 validation accuracy",
    labels = scales::label_percent(),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "CNN validation performance across four settings",
    subtitle = "The selected setting is the point with the highest validation accuracy",
    x = "Adam learning rate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

cnn_model <- cnn_candidates[[best_cnn_index]]$model
cnn_valid_prob <- predict(
  cnn_model, x[valid_idx, , , , drop = FALSE], verbose = 0
)
cnn_valid_pred <- max.col(cnn_valid_prob) - 1L
cnn_valid_accuracy <- mean(cnn_valid_pred == y_writer[valid_idx])

cnn_prob <- predict(
  cnn_model, x[test_idx, , , , drop = FALSE], verbose = 0
)
cnn_pred <- max.col(cnn_prob) - 1L
cnn_truth <- y_writer[test_idx]
cnn_accuracy <- mean(cnn_pred == cnn_truth)
cnn_top3 <- t(apply(cnn_prob, 1, function(probability) {
  order(probability, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3] - 1L
}))
cnn_top3_accuracy <- mean(rowSums(cnn_top3 == cnn_truth) > 0L)
cnn_session_difference <- cnn_accuracy - cnn_valid_accuracy

cnn_session_results <- tibble(
  session = c(4L, 5L),
  role = c("Validation (used for model selection)", "Held-out test"),
  accuracy = c(cnn_valid_accuracy, cnn_accuracy),
  n = c(length(valid_idx), length(test_idx))
)
knitr::kable(
  cnn_session_results,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "CNN accuracy on validation session 4 and held-out test session 5."
)

cnn_by_digit <- tibble(
  digit = metadata$digit[test_idx],
  truth = cnn_truth,
  prediction = cnn_pred
) %>%
  group_by(digit) %>%
  summarise(
    accuracy = mean(truth == prediction),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
knitr::kable(
  cnn_by_digit,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "CNN writer-identification accuracy by digit on session 5."
)

cnn_test_metadata <- metadata[test_idx, ]
aggregate_digit_accuracy <- function(n_digits, n_draws = 1000L) {
  writers <- sort(unique(cnn_test_metadata$person_id))
  correct <- logical(length(writers) * n_draws)
  result_index <- 0L

  for (writer in writers) {
    rows_by_digit <- lapply(0:4, function(digit) {
      which(
        cnn_test_metadata$person_id == writer &
          cnn_test_metadata$digit == digit
      )
    })

    for (draw in seq_len(n_draws)) {
      selected_digits <- sample.int(5L, n_digits)
      selected_rows <- vapply(
        selected_digits,
        function(digit_index) sample(rows_by_digit[[digit_index]], 1L),
        integer(1)
      )
      combined_probability <- colMeans(
        cnn_prob[selected_rows, , drop = FALSE]
      )
      result_index <- result_index + 1L
      correct[result_index] <- which.max(combined_probability) - 1L ==
        as.integer(writer) - 1L
    }
  }

  tibble(
    n_digits = n_digits,
    accuracy = mean(correct)
  )
}

set.seed(5073)
cnn_multi_digit <- map_dfr(1:5, aggregate_digit_accuracy)
```

## Results

The selected CNN achieved `r scales::percent(cnn_accuracy, accuracy = 0.1)` accuracy on session 5, compared with a 5% balanced-class chance rate. The correct writer appeared among the three highest-ranked candidates in `r scales::percent(cnn_top3_accuracy, accuracy = 0.1)` of test images.

Top-three accuracy is not the same as a correct single-writer prediction; it measures how often the correct writer appears on a short candidate list.

The digit-specific results were not identical across digits. In this run, digit `r cnn_by_digit$digit[which.max(cnn_by_digit$accuracy)]` performed best (`r sprintf("%.3f", max(cnn_by_digit$accuracy))`), while digit `r cnn_by_digit$digit[which.min(cnn_by_digit$accuracy)]` was the weakest (`r sprintf("%.3f", min(cnn_by_digit$accuracy))`). Since the test set is balanced, per-digit accuracy gives a simple indication of how useful each digit was for identifying writers in this CNN. It is not a pure measure of writer information: digit-specific shape variation and the model’s limitations may also affect the result.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "CNN writer identification accuracy on the held-out fifth session, shown separately for each digit."
ggplot(cnn_by_digit, aes(x = factor(digit), y = accuracy)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3973ac", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = scales::percent(accuracy, accuracy = 1)),
    vjust = -0.35,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(name = "Digit") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Writer identification accuracy",
    labels = scales::label_percent(),
    limits = c(0, 1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "CNN test accuracy by digit",
    subtitle = "Higher accuracy suggests more writer-discriminative signal in this run"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The table above compares the CNN's accuracy on session 4 and session 5. The held-out test minus validation difference is `r sprintf("%.3f", cnn_session_difference)`. The session-4 result is not an independent estimate because it was used to select the dropout setting; session 5 is the held-out test result. A difference between these scores is consistent with a session shift, but should be interpreted cautiously because it comes from one split and one training run.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "CNN accuracy on validation session 4 and held-out test session 5. The dashed line marks the 5% chance level."
ggplot(cnn_session_results, aes(x = factor(session), y = accuracy, fill = role)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = scales::percent(accuracy, accuracy = 0.1)),
    vjust = -0.4,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#91b5d8", "#3973ac")) +
  scale_x_discrete(name = "Session") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Writer identification accuracy",
    labels = scales::label_percent(),
    limits = c(0, 1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "CNN performance across held-out sessions",
    subtitle = "Session 4 guided model selection; session 5 is the final test"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

This is a closed-set result: the test writers were already known to the model, but their session-5 samples were new to it. That means it does not tell us how the model would do on a completely new person. The row-normalized confusion plot below shows the proportion of each writer’s images assigned to each predicted writer, making consistent confusions easier to spot than in a large count table.

In a second descriptive check, we average the model’s predicted probabilities across randomly selected images of different digits from the same writer in session 5. The plot below shows how identification accuracy changes as more distinct digits are combined. This represents a use case with several images from one person; it does not change the single-image test result above.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "CNN writer identification accuracy after averaging predicted probabilities over one to five distinct digits from the same writer in session 5. Each point averages 1,000 random selections per writer."
ggplot(cnn_multi_digit, aes(x = n_digits, y = accuracy)) +
  geom_line(color = "#3973ac", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(color = "#3973ac", size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Writer identification accuracy",
    labels = scales::label_percent(),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Writer identification with multiple digits",
    x = "Number of different digits combined",
    subtitle = "Predicted probabilities are averaged before choosing the writer"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The images used in each draw are sampled independently from the available replicates for each digit. The resulting curve is a descriptive estimate for this test session and should not be treated as an independent-sample confidence interval.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Row-normalised confusion matrix for CNN predictions on session 5. Diagonal cells are correct predictions."
cnn_confusion <- table(
  true = factor(cnn_truth, levels = 0:19),
  predicted = factor(cnn_pred, levels = 0:19)
)
cnn_confusion_plot <- as.data.frame(cnn_confusion) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  group_by(true) %>%
  mutate(row_share = Freq / sum(Freq)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    true_writer = factor(as.integer(as.character(true)) + 1L, levels = 1:20),
    predicted_writer = factor(
      as.integer(as.character(predicted)) + 1L,
      levels = 1:20
    )
  )

ggplot(cnn_confusion_plot, aes(x = predicted_writer, y = true_writer, fill = row_share)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(levels(cnn_confusion_plot$true_writer))) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "white",
    high = "#245a83",
    labels = scales::label_percent(),
    name = "Share of\ntrue writer"
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "CNN writer confusion on the test session",
    x = "Predicted writer ID",
    y = "True writer ID",
    caption = "Rows are normalised; diagonal cells are correct predictions."
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

# Siamese verification

## Task and pair construction

The task is to decide whether two images were written by the same person. We split writers before constructing pairs: 12 writers for training, four for validation, and four for testing. No validation or test writer appears in training, so this protocol tests verification on writers the model has not seen.

Each pair contains the same digit on both sides to control for digit identity. A positive pair contains different images from the same writer; a negative pair contains images from different writers. Each split has equal numbers of positive and negative pairs. Pairs are sampled across the available sessions.

```{r}
set.seed(5073)
writer_ids <- sample(sort(unique(metadata$person_id)))
train_writers <- writer_ids[1:12]
valid_writers <- writer_ids[13:16]
test_writers  <- writer_ids[17:20]

make_pairs <- function(writers, n_pairs) {
  eligible <- which(metadata$person_id %in% writers)
  available_writers <- sort(unique(metadata$person_id[eligible]))
  labels <- rep(c(1L, 0L), length.out = n_pairs)
  left <- integer(n_pairs)
  right <- integer(n_pairs)

  for (i in seq_len(n_pairs)) {
    digit <- sample(0:4, 1)
    if (labels[i] == 1L) {
      writer <- sample(available_writers, 1)
      candidates <- eligible[
        metadata$person_id[eligible] == writer &
          metadata$digit[eligible] == digit
      ]
      chosen <- sample(candidates, 2)
    } else {
      writers_for_pair <- sample(available_writers, 2)
      first <- eligible[
        metadata$person_id[eligible] == writers_for_pair[1] &
          metadata$digit[eligible] == digit
      ]
      second <- eligible[
        metadata$person_id[eligible] == writers_for_pair[2] &
          metadata$digit[eligible] == digit
      ]
      chosen <- c(sample(first, 1), sample(second, 1))
    }
    left[i] <- chosen[1]
    right[i] <- chosen[2]
  }

  list(left = left, right = right, label = as.numeric(labels))
}

train_pairs <- make_pairs(train_writers, 12000)
valid_pairs <- make_pairs(valid_writers, 2000)
test_pairs  <- make_pairs(test_writers, 2000)

pair_inputs <- function(pairs) {
  list(
    x[pairs$left, , , , drop = FALSE],
    x[pairs$right, , , , drop = FALSE]
  )
}
```

## Network and evaluation

Both inputs pass through the same CNN encoder, which has convolution layers with 32 and 64 filters, two max-pooling steps, and dense layers of 64 and 16 units. The final layer produces a 16-dimensional embedding. We calculate the Euclidean distance between the embeddings and train with contrastive loss,

$$
\begin{aligned}
d &= \left\lVert f(x_a)-f(x_b)\right\rVert_2, \\
\mathcal{L}(y,d) &= y\,d^2 + (1-y)\left[\max(0, m-d)\right]^2,
\qquad m=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $x_a$ and $x_b$ are the two input images, $f(\cdot)$ is the shared encoder, and $y=1$ for a same-writer pair or $y=0$ for a different-writer pair. The margin $m$ is 1 in this analysis. The loss pulls same-writer embeddings together and penalises different-writer embeddings when their distance is less than the margin.

We sampled 12,000 training pairs and 2,000 pairs each for validation and testing. The model uses Adam with a learning rate of 0.001, batches of 128, and early stopping on validation loss for up to 15 epochs.

```{r}
build_siamese <- function(margin = 1) {
  encoder <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(28L, 28L, 1L)) %>%
    layer_conv_2d(32L, 3L, padding = "same", activation = "relu") %>%
    layer_max_pooling_2d(2L) %>%
    layer_conv_2d(64L, 3L, padding = "same", activation = "relu") %>%
    layer_max_pooling_2d(2L) %>%
    layer_flatten() %>%
    layer_dense(64L, activation = "relu") %>%
    layer_dense(16L)

  input_a <- layer_input(shape = c(28L, 28L, 1L))
  input_b <- layer_input(shape = c(28L, 28L, 1L))
  embedding_a <- encoder(input_a)
  embedding_b <- encoder(input_b)
  difference <- layer_subtract(list(embedding_a, embedding_b))

  contrastive_loss <- function(y_true, y_pred) {
    y_true <- op_reshape(y_true, newshape = c(-1L, 1L))
    squared_distance <- op_sum(
      op_square(y_pred), axis = -1L, keepdims = TRUE
    )
    distance <- op_sqrt(squared_distance + 1e-7)
    y_true * squared_distance +
      (1 - y_true) * op_square(op_maximum(margin - distance, 0))
  }

  keras_model(
    inputs = list(input_a, input_b),
    outputs = difference
  ) %>%
    compile(
      optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 0.001),
      loss = contrastive_loss
    )
}

siamese_model <- build_siamese()
siamese_history <- siamese_model %>% fit(
  pair_inputs(train_pairs),
  train_pairs$label,
  validation_data = list(
    pair_inputs(valid_pairs),
    valid_pairs$label
  ),
  epochs = 15,
  batch_size = 128,
  callbacks = list(callback_early_stopping(
    monitor = "val_loss", patience = 3, restore_best_weights = TRUE
  )),
  verbose = 0
)

pair_distances <- function(model, pairs) {
  differences <- predict(model, pair_inputs(pairs), verbose = 0)
  sqrt(rowSums(differences^2) + 1e-7)
}

valid_distance <- pair_distances(siamese_model, valid_pairs)
test_distance <- pair_distances(siamese_model, test_pairs)

balanced_accuracy_at <- function(distance, label, threshold) {
  predicted_match <- distance <= threshold
  sensitivity <- mean(predicted_match[label == 1])
  specificity <- mean(!predicted_match[label == 0])
  (sensitivity + specificity) / 2
}

threshold_grid <- as.numeric(quantile(
  valid_distance, probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = 101)
))
threshold_scores <- map_dbl(
  threshold_grid,
  ~ balanced_accuracy_at(valid_distance, valid_pairs$label, .x)
)
match_threshold <- threshold_grid[which.max(threshold_scores)]

test_match <- test_distance <= match_threshold
test_sensitivity <- mean(test_match[test_pairs$label == 1])
test_specificity <- mean(!test_match[test_pairs$label == 0])
siamese_accuracy <- mean(test_match == (test_pairs$label == 1))
siamese_balanced_accuracy <- (test_sensitivity + test_specificity) / 2
positive_rank_sum <- sum(rank(-test_distance, ties.method = "average")[
  test_pairs$label == 1
])
n_positive <- sum(test_pairs$label == 1)
n_negative <- sum(test_pairs$label == 0)
siamese_auc <- (
  positive_rank_sum - n_positive * (n_positive + 1) / 2
) / (n_positive * n_negative)

test_session_relation <- ifelse(
  metadata$session[test_pairs$left] == metadata$session[test_pairs$right],
  "Same session",
  "Different sessions"
)
siamese_session_results <- tibble(
  session_relation = test_session_relation,
  truth = test_pairs$label,
  predicted = as.integer(test_match)
) %>%
  group_by(session_relation) %>%
  summarise(
    n_pairs = n(),
    accuracy = mean(predicted == truth),
    sensitivity = mean(predicted[truth == 1] == 1),
    specificity = mean(predicted[truth == 0] == 0),
    balanced_accuracy = (sensitivity + specificity) / 2,
    .groups = "drop"
  )
same_session_balanced_accuracy <- siamese_session_results$balanced_accuracy[
  siamese_session_results$session_relation == "Same session"
]
cross_session_balanced_accuracy <- siamese_session_results$balanced_accuracy[
  siamese_session_results$session_relation == "Different sessions"
]
siamese_session_difference <- cross_session_balanced_accuracy -
  same_session_balanced_accuracy

siamese_results <- tibble(
  metric = c("Accuracy", "Balanced accuracy", "Sensitivity (same writer)",
             "Specificity (different writer)", "ROC-AUC",
             "Validation-selected distance threshold"),
  value = c(siamese_accuracy, siamese_balanced_accuracy,
            test_sensitivity, test_specificity, siamese_auc, match_threshold)
)
knitr::kable(
  siamese_results,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Siamese verification metrics on writer-disjoint test pairs."
)
knitr::kable(
  siamese_session_results,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Siamese test results by session relation."
)
```

## Test results

We selected the distance threshold using validation writers only, then applied it unchanged to the held-out test writers. On the test pairs, the model achieved a balanced accuracy of `r sprintf("%.3f", siamese_balanced_accuracy)` and an ROC-AUC of `r sprintf("%.3f", siamese_auc)`. AUC measures how often a randomly selected same-writer pair receives a smaller distance than a different-writer pair; it does not depend on a decision threshold.

Sensitivity is the proportion of same-writer pairs correctly accepted; specificity is the proportion of different-writer pairs correctly rejected. Balanced accuracy averages these two rates, giving equal weight to both pair classes.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Embedding distances for same-writer and different-writer test pairs. The dashed line is the threshold selected on validation writers."
test_distance_plot <- tibble(
  distance = test_distance,
  pair_type = factor(
    test_pairs$label,
    levels = c(1, 0),
    labels = c("Same writer", "Different writers")
  )
)

ggplot(test_distance_plot, aes(x = distance, color = pair_type, fill = pair_type)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.2, adjust = 1) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = match_threshold,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#3973ac", "#c65d3b"), name = "Pair type") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#3973ac", "#c65d3b"), name = "Pair type") +
  labs(
    title = "Siamese distances for held-out writers",
    subtitle = "Distances below the validation-selected threshold are classified as same-writer pairs",
    x = "Euclidean distance between image embeddings",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

For pairs within one session, balanced accuracy was `r sprintf("%.3f", same_session_balanced_accuracy)`; for pairs across sessions, it was `r sprintf("%.3f", cross_session_balanced_accuracy)`, a difference of `r sprintf("%.3f", siamese_session_difference)` (cross-session minus same-session). Both use the same validation-selected threshold. These results describe this sampled set of pairs and four held-out writers; they are not a universal estimate of verification performance.

# Evaluation strategy and leakage

The CNN and Siamese evaluations estimate different forms of generalisation. The CNN uses all 20 writers in training and tests later-session images from those same writers. The Siamese protocol holds out four writers entirely and tests pairs from those unseen writers. The CNN therefore addresses identification from a fixed list, while the Siamese network addresses whether two samples match for writers not used to fit the model.

For the CNN, sessions 1–3 are used for training, session 4 for model selection, and session 5 for the final test. For the Siamese network, writers are assigned to train, validation, and test groups before pairs are formed. This prevents the same writer from crossing those partitions. A random image-level split could place near-identical replicates in both training and test sets, inflating performance; the session- and writer-level splits reduce this risk. Images within a writer–digit–session cell can still be similar, and the sampled pairs share writers and images. Image- and pair-level metrics should therefore not be interpreted as if every observation were independent.

Neither protocol tests performance on real handwriting, new digits, or a larger writer population. The CNN’s fixed candidate list and the Siamese network’s four test writers also constrain how broadly the results can be generalised.

# Hyperparameter optimisation

For the CNN, we compared a 2 × 2 grid of dropout rates (0.2 and 0.4) and Adam learning rates (0.001 and 0.0005). Each configuration was trained with the same random seed and early stopping on session-4 validation accuracy. The table reports each setting’s best validation accuracy, validation loss at that epoch, and best epoch. We chose the setting with the highest validation accuracy and evaluated it on session 5 only after that choice.

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  cnn_tuning %>%
    mutate(learning_rate = formatC(learning_rate, format = "f", digits = 4)),
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c(
    "Dropout",
    "Adam learning rate",
    "Best validation accuracy",
    "Validation loss at best accuracy",
    "Best epoch",
    "Selected"
  ),
  caption = "CNN tuning results on the session-4 validation set."
)
```

Validation accuracy varied by `r scales::percent(diff(range(cnn_tuning$best_validation_accuracy)), accuracy = 0.1)` across the four settings. This small search does not isolate the effect of either parameter, and one seed per setting does not measure seed variability. We held the Siamese architecture and margin fixed; its test results were not used to tune either model.

# Comparison and critical discussion

The CNN performs closed-set identification: it chooses one of the 20 writers seen during training. Its session-5 accuracy was `r scales::percent(cnn_accuracy, accuracy = 0.1)`. The Siamese model performs verification on pairs from writers excluded from training, achieving `r scales::percent(siamese_balanced_accuracy, accuracy = 0.1)` balanced accuracy. These scores are not directly comparable: the tasks, class counts, and test populations differ.

The CNN’s digit-specific results and multi-digit aggregation describe performance on this split. They do not establish that one digit is consistently more informative, or that the estimated improvement from combining digits would carry over to a new sample. The Siamese pair construction controls for digit identity by comparing images of the same digit.

The CNN validation and test results compare sessions 4 and 5; the Siamese table compares same-session and cross-session test pairs. These are descriptive comparisons from one split and training run. They do not establish that session changes alone caused any performance difference.

# Limitations {.unnumbered}

- The images are simulated and cover only five digits; results may not transfer to real handwriting or other writing tasks.
- There are 20 writers, and the writer-disjoint Siamese test set contains only four. Its estimates may depend strongly on which writers are held out.
- Images within a writer–digit–session cell and sampled pairs sharing images or writers are related observations. The nominal image and pair counts overstate the amount of independent information.
- The CNN search covers four settings, with one random seed per setting. It does not measure seed variability or the effect of other architectural choices.
- Multi-digit accuracy is estimated from repeated draws of the same session-5 images. It is descriptive, not an independent test set.
- The CNN and Siamese results target different forms of generalisation and should not be ranked against each other.

# Conclusion {.unnumbered}

On session 5, the CNN identified known writers with `r scales::percent(cnn_accuracy, accuracy = 0.1)` single-image accuracy. Combining all five digits gave `r scales::percent(cnn_multi_digit$accuracy[5], accuracy = 0.1)` accuracy in the repeated-draw check. On pairs from four writers held out from Siamese training, the verifier achieved `r sprintf("%.3f", siamese_auc)` ROC-AUC and `r scales::percent(siamese_balanced_accuracy, accuracy = 0.1)` balanced accuracy at a threshold selected on validation writers. These results answer different questions and apply to this simulated dataset and its splits. Related replicates, a small writer population, and session differences limit how confidently the metrics can be generalised.
